audit_scope.description: Trust model analysis for Ethereum Execution Layer focusing on external entities that interact with the EL through various interfaces.

misclassified_entities.reason: Smart contracts on-chain are part of the system, not external entities. They execute within the EVM and are under the control of the Execution Layer.
Hardware wallets are external to Ethereum infrastructure but do not directly interact with the system boundary. They sign transactions offline which are then submitted by users.
Off-chain verifiers are read-only consumers of blockchain data; they do not send data into the system boundary and therefore are not trust-relevant external entities.
The Ethereum client/EVM is the system being audited, not an external entity. This should be considered an internal component.
The EVM opcode dispatcher is an internal component of the EVM, not an external entity.
Contract execution context is an internal EVM state, not an external entity.
Smart contracts executing within the EVM are internal to the system, not external entities.
Contracts calling precompiles are internal to the EVM, not external entities.
Client implementation teams do not interact with the running system; they develop the software. Not a runtime external entity.
Core developers do not interact with the running system at runtime; they define protocol changes. Not a runtime external entity.
EIP authors do not interact with the running system at runtime. Not a runtime external entity.
The deposit contract is a smart contract executing within the EVM, making it an internal component, not an external entity.

trusted_external_entities.name: Transaction Submitter via JSON-RPC
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Users submit transactions through unauthenticated JSON-RPC endpoints. All transaction data must be validated: signature verification, nonce checks, balance checks, gas limit validation, and EVM execution sandboxing.

trusted_external_entities.name: Transaction Submitter via P2P or JSON-RPC
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: P2P transaction gossip and JSON-RPC API
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Transaction submitters can be anyone on the network. Transactions arrive via unauthenticated channels (P2P gossip or JSON-RPC) and must undergo full validation including signature verification, type validation, and payload structure checks.

trusted_external_entities.name: Transaction Signer
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Transaction signers prove ownership of accounts via ECDSA signatures. While signatures provide authentication, the transaction content itself is untrusted and must be validated. Signature verification prevents impersonation but not malicious transaction content.

trusted_external_entities.name: P2P Gossip Network
trusted_external_entities.rationale: P2P network peers are unauthenticated and untrusted. All data received via gossip (blocks, transactions, SSZ data) must be fully validated. Length validation prevents DoS attacks from oversized messages.

trusted_external_entities.name: Network Peer (Block Propagation)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Network peers propagate blocks via unauthenticated P2P protocol. Blocks must undergo full validation: header checks, PoW/PoS verification, state root validation, transaction execution, and merkle root verification.

trusted_external_entities.name: Network Peer (General P2P)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Network peers can be malicious actors attempting to send invalid data, cause DoS, or exploit consensus bugs. All P2P data must be validated before processing.

trusted_external_entities.name: Node Operators
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Node operators run EL clients and participate in P2P networking. They are untrusted in the Byzantine fault tolerant model - some operators may be malicious, misconfigured, or compromised. The protocol must function correctly despite presence of malicious operators.

trusted_external_entities.name: Transaction Sender (EOA)
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Signed transactions via P2P or JSON-RPC
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Transaction senders are externally owned accounts (EOAs) that sign transactions. While ECDSA signatures provide authentication, senders are untrusted and may attempt malicious transactions, reentrancy attacks, or resource exhaustion. All transaction content must be validated and executed in sandboxed EVM environment.

trusted_external_entities.name: Block Miner (PoW)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Miners produce blocks and select transactions, creating opportunities for censorship, MEV extraction, and reordering attacks. PoW provides Sybil resistance but does not prevent malicious block content. All proposed blocks must be fully validated by all nodes.

trusted_external_entities.name: Consensus Layer via Engine API
trusted_external_entities.rationale: The Consensus Layer communicates with the Execution Layer via the Engine API using JWT authentication. The channel is authenticated but the content (block proposals, fork choice updates) requires validation. The CL could be compromised or malicious, so the EL must validate all payloads: transaction validity, state transitions, gas limits, and consensus rules.

boundary_edges.security_assumption: All user-submitted transactions are treated as untrusted. The EL validates signatures, nonces, balances, gas limits, and executes in sandboxed EVM with gas metering.

Transaction submitters are untrusted. All transactions undergo signature verification, type validation (EIP-2718), payload structure validation, and mempool acceptance rules before propagation or inclusion.

Signatures provide authentication but not authorization. The EL verifies ECDSA signatures to authenticate transaction origin, but must still validate all transaction content (nonce, balance, gas, calldata) and execute defensively.
P2P gossip data is untrusted. All serialized data (SSZ, RLP) undergoes length validation before deserialization to prevent DoS. Transaction and block validation rules are applied before propagation.

Blocks from peers are untrusted. The EL performs full validation: header validation, PoW/PoS verification, transaction execution, state root computation, receipt root verification, and consensus rule enforcement.

P2P peers are Byzantine actors in the threat model. All data from peers (blocks, transactions, state sync data) is validated before processing. Rate limiting and peer reputation systems mitigate DoS attacks.

Node operators are untrusted. The protocol assumes Byzantine fault tolerance where up to f < n/3 nodes can be malicious. Consensus rules and validation ensure protocol safety despite malicious operators.

EOA senders are untrusted. The EL validates sender has no code (is EOA), checks nonce matches account state, verifies sufficient balance for gas*price+value, and executes transaction in isolated EVM context with gas metering and stack depth limits.

Miners are untrusted block producers. The EL validates PoW (hashimoto_light), difficulty target, block header fields, transaction validity, gas limits, state transitions, and merkle roots. Miners cannot violate consensus rules without other nodes rejecting the block.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Engine API (authenticated with JWT over HTTP/JSON-RPC)
boundary_edges.security_assumption: The CL is semi-trusted with authenticated channel (JWT) but untrusted content. The EL validates all Engine API payloads: block proposals undergo full transaction validation, state root computation, and gas limit checks. Fork choice updates are validated for consistency with known chain state.
